newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. trade gap seen stifling GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. trade gap seen stifling GDP growth.

text.p: The persistent failure of U.S. exports to keep pace with imports could take some of the steam out of overall gross domestic product (GDP) growth in coming months, analysts said.
A weak global economy and the dollar's persistent strength in foreign exchange markets should prevent the portly U.S. trade gap from slimming down in the near term, analysts said.
That reality has tempered some of the optimism in economists' 1997 GDP forecasts.
"That's not very good. Export growth has slowed down quite a bit and we're still seeing economic weakness among our trading partners in Europe and Japan," McGee added.
The bilateral trade gap with Japan steadily shrank earlier this year, but that trend seems to have ended.

Japan on Wednesday reported its November trade data, which showed the gap with the U.S. swelling by 30 percent to $3.31 billion from a year ago. Japan's Ministry of Finance cited a 46 percent rise in car exports to the U.S. and economists blamed the strong dollar, which makes Japanese exports to the U.S. cheaper.

"Normally this far into the business cycle, you would expect a little more contribution from trade, but unless we get a pick-up (in global demand), next year will be a disappointment," said Tim McGee, international economist at Tokai Bank.
Analysts will get the latest snapshot on U.S. trade on Thursday when the Commerce Department releases international trade figures for October.
The consensus Reuters poll forecast is for a $10.4 billion shortfall, which would represent a dip from the whopping $11.3 billion gap in September, but still show a glaring problem.

"We're basically looking for both imports and exports to be somewhat sluggish, but we're growing much better than most of our trading partners and that keeps the overall gap at these wide levels," said Richard Koss, international strategist at MFR Inc.

Most analysts see U.S. GDP growth of about 2.0 percent in 1997. While far from robust, that expansion could easily exceed growth in Japan, which has suffered a deep economic malaise for several years, and continental Europe, where tight fiscal policy is severely restricting demand.
That should help preserve the dollar's recent gains, analysts said.
"The short-term fundamentals and interest rate differentials are supportive for the dollar," said Koss.
U.S. firms have generally found ways to compete overseas despite the firm dollar. But without stronger foreign demand, the trade disparity should continue to widen, analysts said.

"We are at a competitive disadvantage with Japan, but we're probably not too bad in Europe. If we saw some growth overseas, you'd see the trade gap narrow. The problem is we don't see a lot of growth in the first half of 1997," Koss said.
